content:
Hello,

I played with coroutines in lean, i surprisingly implemented the python equivalent of generators in just a few lines of code. The implementation is tail-recusive so it should not blow your stack.
Full source code in gist with link to playgound

It looks like this when using it :

def fibonacci : Coroutine Nat Unit := do
  let mut a := 0
  let mut b := 1
  repeat
    yield a
    (a, b) := (b, a + b)

/--
info: #[1, 2, 2, 3, 4, 6, 9, 14, 22, 35]
-/
#guard_msgs in
#eval fibonacci
  |>.map (· + 1)
  |>.take 10
  |>.toArray

What's nice about this implementation, is that implementing all combinators is really easy and readable using do notation :

/--
Map a function over the yielded values of a coroutine.
-/
def map {α : Type v} {β : Type w} (f : α → β) (c : Coroutine α Unit) : Coroutine β Unit := do
  for o in c do
    yield (f o)

It could be an easier (for functional programmers) alternative to iterators that we currently have.

I benchmarked some basic tests.
Running a simple coroutine that generate millions of nats versus the equivalent with iterators.
The performance is almost the same with a small advantage for this coroutine, but i can't say it's conclusive.
They are doing the same thing, with almost the same structure (an inductive type with a state)
Implementation wise, they are not doing the same thing. Iterators are much more complex to implement.
compare iterator version from the docs:

structure Nats where
  next : Nat

instance [Pure m] : Iterator Nats m Nat where
  IsPlausibleStep it
    | .yield it' n =>
      n = it.internalState.next ∧
      it'.internalState.next = n + 1
    | _ => False
  step it :=
    let n := it.internalState.next
    pure <| .deflate <|
      .yield { it with internalState.next := n + 1 } n (by grind)

instance [Pure m] [Monad n] : IteratorLoop Nats m n :=
  .defaultImplementation

instance [Pure m] : Productive Nats m where
  wf := .intro <| fun _ => .intro _ nofun

def Nats.iter : Iter (α := Nats) Nat :=
  IterM.mk { next := 0 } |>.toIter

versus coroutines version :

def nats : Coroutine Nat Unit := do
  let mut n := 0
  repeat
    yield n
    n := n + 1

For much more complex use cases, coroutines (if you only care about programming ergonomics) can be a performant alternative to iterators.
If there is any desire, i can make it a full fledge library listed in reservoir.

The performance is almost the same with a small advantage for this coroutine, but i can't say it's conclusive.

The performance of a coroutine library with the design you have above cannot compete with the iterator library, given how our code generator work at the moment. Take as a simple example:

def cor (n : Nat) : Array Nat :=
  nats |>.take n |>.map (· * 59) |>.filter (· % 2 == 0) |>.toArray

def iter (n : Nat) : Array Nat :=
  Nats.iter |>.take n |>.map (· * 59) |>.filter (· % 2 == 0) |>.toArray

#time #eval (cor 1_000_000).size
#time #eval (iter 1_000_000).size

we have

coroutine: time: 8846ms
iterators: time: 512ms

so almost a 20x difference, potentially even more if this is compiled to native code. Your design approach unfortunately introduces a lot of closure allocation /deallocation and chasing which the standard library iterator API does not.
interresting, i did my timings with release mode, not #time and #eval. but maybe i did it wrong, i'll recheck.
If you did them using a compiled binary your results may well have been constant lifted depending on how you set up your benchmark which would invalidate them.
that would explain it. thanks for the insight.
Note that the iterators code still produces suboptimal code as well and in subsequent Lean releases we are likely going to be able to squeeze quite a bit more out of this.

The loop is currently

              return _x.16

but really it should be

def _private.Init.WFExtrinsicFix.0.WellFounded.opaqueFix₂._at_.iter.spec_0._redArg countdown inner b : obj :=
      let _x.4 := 1;
      let _x.5 := Nat.decEq countdown _x.4;
      cases _x.5 : obj
      | Bool.false =>
        let _x.6 := Nat.add inner _x.4;
        let _x.7 := Nat.sub countdown _x.4;
        dec countdown;
        let _x.10 := 59;
        let _x.11 := Nat.mul inner _x.10;
        dec inner;
        let _x.12 := 2;
        let _x.13 := Nat.mod _x.11 _x.12;
        let _x.14 := 0;
        let _x.15 := Nat.decEq _x.13 _x.14;
        dec _x.13;
        cases _x.15 : obj
        | Bool.false =>
          dec _x.11;
          let _x.16 := _private.Init.WFExtrinsicFix.0.WellFounded.opaqueFix₂._at_.iter.spec_0._redArg _x.6 _x.7 b;
          return _x.16
        | Bool.true =>
          let _x.17 := Array.push ◾ b _x.11;
          let _x.18 := _private.Init.WFExtrinsicFix.0.WellFounded.opaqueFix₂._at_.iter.spec_0._redArg _x.6 _x.7 _x.17;
          return _x.18;
      | Bool.true =>
        dec inner;
        dec countdown;
        return b;

I did the test on my computer using #time on the same exemple, i don't have X20, but indeed it's slower :

cor : time: 842ms
iter: time: 504ms
Ok, but if i make it generate even larger batch, i start to have timing grow more exponentially while iterator timings grow linearly. So maybe memory cache or something is in play.
After digging, there is indeed a threshold where coroutine is faster than iterator (and it may depend on the computer) then it becomes slower until it gets badly worse.
